## What you will do

A digital twin is not a random person. It is **a slot in a measured population
frame**, filled by a record and then given attitudes by a matched survey
respondent. This notebook builds the frame and fills 400 of those slots for
Ohio, then audits what you drew.

By the end you will have:

1. read a **stage-1 frame** — who lives in each Ohio district, from the ACS;
2. read a **stage-2 frame** — how each of those cells voted in November 2024;
3. checked the frame against the **certified** 2024 result;
4. collapsed it to a **teaching mini-frame**;
5. drawn **400 synthetic skeletons** by probability-proportional-to-size sampling;
6. **audited** the drawn margins, and raked them to the acceptance standard.

Nothing here calls a language model. That is the point: *the composition of a
panel is fixed by census and certified-result data before any model is
involved.* The model never chooses who is in the panel.

> **A note on what you are drawing.** There are two routes to a skeleton. The
> stronger one starts from a state **voter file**: the official list of
> registered voters, with each person's county, registration and turnout
> history. Ohio publishes one, and the Talking to Machines panel draws **real
> registrants** from it into these cells. Working with a voter file requires a
> licence and ethical care, because every row is a real, identifiable person.
> This notebook takes the other route: it draws **synthetic skeletons**
> directly from the census frame. Section 7 shows what the registrant route adds.

**How to read this notebook.** Every table and figure the code prints has a
number (Table 1.1, Figure 1.1, …), given in bold just above the code that prints
it. When the text quotes a number, it says which table it comes from, and which
row or column to look at.

The first block loads the three R packages the notebook uses and fixes the
random seed, so everyone draws the same panel.

```{r libs}
library(arrow)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

DATA <- file.path("..", "data")
set.seed(20261013L)   # every draw in this notebook is seeded and reproducible
```

## 1. Stage 1 — who lives here

Stage 1 is the American Community Survey (ACS) 2019–2023 five-year PUMS: the
individual responses behind the ACS, for adults 18+, allocated from their PUMA
(the smallest area the ACS publishes) to congressional districts.

The block below loads it as a table called `sf1`, prints its size (rows,
columns), and prints its first three rows.

**Table 1.1.** `sf1`, the stage-1 frame: size, then the first three rows.

```{r stage1}
sf1 <- as.data.table(read_parquet(file.path(DATA, "SF_OH.parquet")))
dim(sf1)
head(sf1, 3)
```

Each row of Table 1.1 is a **cell**: one combination of district (`CD119`),
sex, ethnicity, age band, marital status, degree, household income, internet
access and citizenship. The line above the table gives the size: 23,798 cells
and 12 columns. The last two columns are the ones that matter:

- `n_pums` is how many ACS respondents fall in the cell (640 in the first row);
- `N` is how many Ohio adults those respondents stand for (9,950 in the first
  row). Each respondent carries a **person weight**, the number of people they
  represent, and `N` is the sum of those weights.

The ACS is a sample, but the Census Bureau calibrates its person weights to
independent population controls. So adding up `N` reproduces the **ACS's own
published estimates** for Ohio directly, without raking afterwards. They are
estimates, with sampling error, not a census count.

The next block adds up `N` over all cells, and over citizens only (`citizen == 1`).

**Table 1.2.** `sf1` summed: number of cells, adults, and citizen adults.

```{r stage1-totals}
sf1[, .(cells = .N,
        adults = format(sum(N), big.mark = ","),
        citizen_adults = format(sum(N[citizen == 1]), big.mark = ","))]
```

Table 1.2 shows 9,170,227 adults, of whom 8,931,251 are citizens (column
`citizen_adults`). Everything from stage 2 on uses the **citizen adults**, the
people who can vote. The same 8,931,251 is the size of the frame Notebook 3
post-stratifies to.

## 2. Stage 2 — how those cells voted

Stage 1 says who lives in a district. Stage 2 says **how each cell voted in
November 2024**, in four classes: Democratic, Republican, other, and stayed
home.

It is a multinomial logit fitted in Stan over the CES 2024 vote-validated
release, with the certified district result as an area predictor and
hierarchical effects for sex, ethnicity, college, age, income, state and
district. Model probabilities are then computed for every stage-1 cell and
**raked** within each district so that D, R, other and stay-home totals equal
the certified result.

You do not fit this model here. It was fitted once, and this notebook reads its
result: `SF_extended_OH.parquet`, the stage-1 cells with the four vote classes
attached.

The block below loads it as `sf2` and prints its size and first three rows.

**Table 1.3.** `sf2`, the stage-2 frame: size, then the first three rows.

```{r stage2}
sf2 <- as.data.table(read_parquet(file.path(DATA, "SF_extended_OH.parquet")))
dim(sf2)
head(sf2, 3)
```

`sf2` has 9,467 rows (the line above Table 1.3). It keeps **citizens only**, and
drops marital status and internet access from the key, so it has fewer cells
than `sf1`. The district is now in the column `area` (`OH-01`, …). `N` is still
the number of citizen adults in the cell, and each row gains two sets of
columns:

- `p_D`, `p_R`, `p_Other`, `p_stay home`: the model's probability that a person
  in this cell voted Democratic, Republican, other, or stayed home;
- `N_D`, `N_R`, `N_Other`, `N_stay`: how many of the cell's `N` people fall in
  each class, after raking to the certified result.

In the first row of Table 1.3, 4,832 men aged 18–24 in OH-01 split into about
78 Democratic voters, 458 Republican, 19 other and 4,277 who stayed home.

The four counts split `N` between them, so they must add back up to it. The
next block prints the largest gap between `N_D + N_R + N_Other + N_stay` and
`N` across all 9,467 rows:

```{r stage2-check-rowsum}
# the four counts should sum back to the cell size
sf2[, max(abs(N_D + N_R + N_Other + N_stay - N))]
```

The answer is of the order of 0.0000000001: rounding, so the counts add up.

## 3. Does the frame know the answer? Check it against certified results

This is the first validation the project runs on every frame. After raking, district totals
are exact *by construction* — so the honest check is whether the numbers you
have match the certified results you were raked to, and whether the **shape**
of the vote across districts is right.

The first block loads the certified 2024 presidential result by district as
`cert`, and prints Harris's two-party share for Ohio's 15 districts.

**Table 1.4.** `cert`: the certified 2024 result. `certified_harris_2p` is
Harris's share of the two-party (Harris + Trump) vote; `cvap` is the district's
citizen voting-age population.

```{r certified}
cert <- fread(file.path(DATA, "predictor_cd119_2024.csv"),
              colClasses = list(character = "CD119"))[state == "OH"]
cert[, .(CD119, certified_harris_2p = 1 - pct_trump, cvap)][order(CD119)]
```

The next block computes the same share from the frame: for each district, the
Democratic voters in `sf2` over its Democratic plus Republican voters. It puts
the two side by side in a table called `cmp`, with the difference in percentage
points.

**Table 1.5.** `cmp`: frame against certified, by district. `diff_pp` is the
frame minus the certified share, in points.

```{r frame-vs-certified}
byCD <- sf2[, .(frame_harris_2p = sum(N_D) / sum(N_D + N_R)), by = .(CD119 = sub("OH-", "", area))]
cmp  <- merge(byCD, cert[, .(CD119, certified_harris_2p = 1 - pct_trump)], by = "CD119")
cmp[, diff_pp := 100 * (frame_harris_2p - certified_harris_2p)]
cmp[order(CD119)]
```

Every value in the `diff_pp` column of Table 1.5 is about 0.00001 points: the
frame reproduces the certified result exactly. The last block plots the same
two columns against each other, saves the plot to `figures/`, and shows it.

**Figure 1.1.** Frame against certified Harris share, one point per district.

```{r frame-vs-certified-plot}
p_frame <- ggplot(cmp, aes(100 * certified_harris_2p, 100 * frame_harris_2p)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, colour = "#2c6e9e") +
  geom_text(aes(label = CD119), nudge_y = 1.1, size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "Certified Harris share, two-party (%)",
       y = "Frame Harris share, two-party (%)",
       title = "Ohio stage-2 frame against the certified 2024 result",
       subtitle = "Exact by construction after raking — this checks the rake, not the model") +
  coord_equal() + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggsave(file.path("..", "figures", "oh_frame_vs_certified.png"), p_frame,
       width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 200)
p_frame
```

> **Discussion.** Why is Figure 1.1 *not* evidence that the method works? What
> would be? (The answer: a held-out election —
> New Jersey, November 2025 — that appears nowhere in the pipeline. We come back
> to it in Notebook 3.)

## 4. The mini-frame

The project's registrant draw uses `district × county × sex × ethnicity × age` as its
cell key, with the vote class assigned inside each cell. **County is not in the
ACS frame** — it enters only from the voter file, which splits each frame cell
across counties by its own composition. Since you are drawing synthetically,
your key is:

```
district × sex × ethnicity × age × college × vote2024
```

The mini-frame is **not a subset**. It holds the same citizen adults as `sf2`,
under a different key: the vote class moves from four count columns (`N_D`,
`N_R`, `N_Other`, `N_stay`) into the key, and household income drops out. Same
people, re-keyed.

Why can a synthetic draw not have county? The ACS does not publish it. The
smallest geography in the PUMS is the PUMA, and PUMAs and counties do not nest:
a rural PUMA combines several whole counties, and an urban county is split
across several PUMAs. Placing a synthetic person in a county would mean
inventing that joint distribution. A voter file records each registrant's county
directly.

This is worth pausing on. Leaving county out is a real defect. When the
project's panels were drawn without it, a county's realised partisan
composition was an uncontrolled by-product of the draw, and Passaic County, New
Jersey came out **13.4 points too Democratic**. Adding county to the cell key
brought the state's county error from 2.98 to 1.73 points. Your
synthetic sample cannot have this control, and it is the clearest illustration
of what a voter file buys you.

The block below builds the mini-frame as a table called `mini`. It turns each
`sf2` row into four rows, one per vote class, each with that class's count as
its `N`; drops the empty ones; adds up rows that now share the same key (which
is where income disappears); and sorts them. It prints the number of cells and
people, then the first five rows.

**Table 1.6.** `mini`, the mini-frame: size, then the first five cells.

```{r miniframe}
mini <- melt(
  sf2,
  id.vars      = c("area", "gender", "ethnicity", "age_bins", "college_grad"),
  measure.vars = c("N_D", "N_R", "N_Other", "N_stay"),
  variable.name = "vote2024", value.name = "N"
)
mini[, vote2024 := factor(vote2024, levels = c("N_D", "N_R", "N_Other", "N_stay"),
                                    labels = c("D", "R", "Other", "stay"))]
mini <- mini[N > 0, .(N = sum(N)), by = .(cd = area, gender, ethnicity, age_bins,
                                          college_grad, vote2024)]
setorder(mini, cd, vote2024, ethnicity, age_bins, gender)

cat(sprintf("%s cells, %s citizen adults\n",
            format(nrow(mini), big.mark = ","), format(round(sum(mini$N)), big.mark = ",")))
head(mini, 5)
```

The line above Table 1.6 confirms it: 9,540 cells holding the same 8,931,251
citizen adults as `sf2`. Each row is a cell of the key above, and `N` is the
number of people in it: the first row is 14 Asian women aged 18–24 without a
degree in OH-01 who voted Democratic.

## 5. Draw 400 skeletons

**Systematic probability-proportional-to-size.** Sort the cells, take the
cumulative population, lay down 400 equally spaced points along it, and take the
cell each point lands in. Compared with drawing 400 independent cells this gives
margins on the leading sort keys that are exact to ±1 — which is why the
project's draw uses it.

The block below writes that procedure as a function, `draw_pps()`, and runs it
on `mini` to draw 400 skeletons into a table called `panel`. Inside the
function: `step` is the population between two picks; `start` is a random
point inside the first step; `picks` are the 400 equally spaced points;
`cum` is the running total of `N` down the sorted cells; and `findInterval()`
finds the cell each point lands in. Each pick gets an id, `oh_syn_0001` to
`oh_syn_0400`. The block prints the size of `panel` and its first five rows.

**Table 1.7.** `panel`, your 400 skeletons: size, then the first five.

```{r draw}
draw_pps <- function(frame, n, seed = 20261013L) {
  set.seed(seed)
  f    <- copy(frame)[N > 0]
  step <- sum(f$N) / n
  start <- runif(1, 0, step)
  picks <- start + step * (0:(n - 1))
  f[, cum := cumsum(N)]
  idx  <- findInterval(picks, c(0, f$cum), rightmost.closed = TRUE)
  out  <- f[idx]
  out[, `:=`(cum = NULL, N = NULL)]
  out[, twin_id := sprintf("oh_syn_%04d", seq_len(.N))]
  setcolorder(out, "twin_id")
  out[]
}

panel <- draw_pps(mini, n = 400)
dim(panel)
head(panel, 5)
```

Each row of Table 1.7 is one skeleton: the attributes of the cell its pick
landed in, and nothing else.

To picture the draw, the next block prints its arithmetic: the population
between two picks, the median and largest cell, how many cells are bigger than
one step (and so certain to be picked), and how many distinct cells the 400
picks landed in.

**Table 1.8.** The draw in numbers.

```{r draw-numbers}
data.table(people            = round(sum(mini$N)),
           people_per_pick   = round(sum(mini$N) / 400),
           median_cell       = round(median(mini$N)),
           largest_cell      = round(max(mini$N)),
           cells_above_step  = sum(mini$N >= sum(mini$N) / 400),
           distinct_cells    = uniqueN(panel, by = c("cd", "gender", "ethnicity", "age_bins",
                                                     "college_grad", "vote2024")))
```

Read Table 1.8 from left to right. 8,931,251 people over 400 picks is one pick
every 22,328 people (`people_per_pick`). The cells are sorted, their populations
added up into a running total, the first point falls at random inside the first
22,328, and each later point is one step further on. The median cell holds 50
people and the largest about 40,000, so only the 32 cells bigger than one step
(`cells_above_step`) are certain to be picked. The 400 picks land in 389
distinct cells (`distinct_cells`): a few cells were picked twice.

> **A pick is a person, not a cell.** The cell supplies the attributes; the pick
> is one individual drawn from it. Two picks in the same cell are two different
> people who happen to share a profile. The rest of the workshop rests on this:
> each of your 400 skeletons stands for one Ohioan.

Each skeleton then gets an integer age drawn uniformly within its band: 18–24
from 18 to 24, and 65+ from 65 to 89. That puts the average 65+ skeleton at 77,
older than Ohio's real 65+ population. No margin changes, since the band is what
gets raked, but every persona that states an age inherits it. The civic record
is rendered explicitly as **not observed** — a synthetic skeleton has no turnout
history, and the persona must say so rather than invent one.

The block below adds both columns to `panel` (`age_lo` and `age_hi` are the
ends of each band) and prints the first five skeletons again.

**Table 1.9.** `panel` with ages, first five skeletons.

```{r ages}
age_lo <- c("18-24" = 18, "25-34" = 25, "35-44" = 35, "45-54" = 45, "55-64" = 55, "65+" = 65)
age_hi <- c("18-24" = 24, "25-34" = 34, "35-44" = 44, "45-54" = 54, "55-64" = 64, "65+" = 89)
panel[, age := mapply(function(a) sample(age_lo[[a]]:age_hi[[a]], 1), age_bins)]
panel[, civic_record := "not observed (synthetic skeleton drawn from the ACS frame)"]
head(panel[, .(twin_id, cd, gender, ethnicity, age, college_grad, vote2024)], 5)
```

## 6. Audit what you drew

A panel is only useful if it is the electorate in miniature. The project's
acceptance standard is: **every one-way margin within 0.3 percentage points
unweighted, and 0.00 weighted, with no cell short.**

A **one-way margin** is the share of the panel in each category of one
variable: the share that is female, the share in each age band, and so on. The
audit compares your panel with the mini-frame. The mini-frame is `sf2`
re-keyed, so its one-way margins are the full frame's: this is your panel
against the Ohio frame.

The block below writes the comparison as a function, `margin_check()`. For one
variable it computes the share of `panel` in each category (`panel_share`), the
share of `mini`'s people in the same category (`frame_share`), and the
difference in points (`diff_pp`). It then runs it for the five audited variables
and prints only the largest gap for each.

**Table 1.10.** The audit, largest gap per variable (in percentage points).

```{r audit-fn}
margin_check <- function(panel, frame, var) {
  p <- panel[, .(panel_share = .N / nrow(panel)), by = var]
  f <- frame[, .(frame_share = sum(N) / sum(frame$N)), by = var]
  m <- merge(p, f, by = var, all = TRUE)
  m[is.na(panel_share), panel_share := 0][is.na(frame_share), frame_share := 0]
  m[, diff_pp := 100 * (panel_share - frame_share)]
  m[order(-abs(diff_pp))]
}

for (v in c("gender", "ethnicity", "age_bins", "vote2024", "cd")) {
  cat("\n---", v, "— max |diff| =",
      sprintf("%.2f pp\n", max(abs(margin_check(panel, mini, v)$diff_pp))))
}
```

Table 1.10 shows that only the district margin (`cd`, 0.23 points) clears the
0.3-point bar; sex, ethnicity, age and vote class do not. The next block prints
the full comparison for two of them, every category, largest gap first.

**Tables 1.11 and 1.12.** Vote class, then ethnicity: panel against frame.

```{r audit-detail}
margin_check(panel, mini, "vote2024")
margin_check(panel, mini, "ethnicity")
```

The first row of Table 1.11 is the one to notice: `Other` has a `panel_share` of
0 against a `frame_share` of 0.0057. The frame has third-party voters; your
panel has none.

The next block re-runs the draw at `n = 4000`, the project's Tier C size, and
stores it as `panel_4000`. It prints nothing; Exercise 6.1 and the rest of this
section use it.

```{r draw-4000}
panel_4000 <- draw_pps(mini, n = 4000)
```

### Raking the residual away

Systematic PPS leaves rounding residue on the margins that are not the leading
sort key. **Raking** removes it: each skeleton gets a weight, and the weights
are adjusted one variable at a time, round after round, until the weighted
shares match the frame's.

The block below defines three functions: `rake()` computes the weights;
`wmargin()` is the weighted version of the margin check; `report()` prints the
range of the weights and the largest weighted gap for each variable. It then
rakes `panel` on the five variables, stores the result in a new column,
`weight`, and prints the report.

**Table 1.13.** The raked 400-skeleton panel: weight range, then the largest
weighted gap per variable.

```{r rake}
rake <- function(panel, frame, vars, iters = 50) {
  w <- rep(1, nrow(panel))
  for (i in seq_len(iters)) {
    for (v in vars) {
      tgt <- frame[, .(t = sum(N) / sum(frame$N)), by = v]
      cur <- data.table(lvl = panel[[v]], w = w)[, .(c = sum(w)), by = lvl][, c := c / sum(c)]
      setnames(cur, "lvl", v)
      f <- merge(cur, tgt, by = v)[, ratio := t / c]
      w <- w * f$ratio[match(panel[[v]], f[[v]])]
    }
  }
  w / mean(w)
}

MARGINS <- c("gender", "ethnicity", "age_bins", "vote2024", "cd")

wmargin <- function(panel, frame, var) {
  p <- panel[, .(panel_share = sum(weight) / sum(panel$weight)), by = var]
  f <- frame[, .(frame_share = sum(N) / sum(frame$N)), by = var]
  merge(p, f, by = var, all = TRUE)[is.na(panel_share), panel_share := 0
    ][, max(abs(100 * (panel_share - frame_share)))]
}

report <- function(panel, frame, label) {
  cat(label, sprintf("— weights %.2f–%.2f\n", min(panel$weight), max(panel$weight)))
  for (v in MARGINS)
    cat(sprintf("   %-10s weighted max |diff| = %.4f pp\n", v, wmargin(panel, frame, v)))
}

panel[, weight := rake(panel, mini, MARGINS)]
report(panel, mini, "n = 400")
```

In Table 1.13, two margins do not reach zero: `ethnicity` and `vote2024`. That
is not a bug in the raking — it is a property of the sample you drew. The next
block counts the skeletons in each vote class:

**Table 1.14.** `panel`: skeletons per 2024 vote class.

```{r why-residual}
panel[, .N, by = vote2024][order(vote2024)]
```

Table 1.14 has no `Other` row: there are **no `Other`-class twins at all**.
Other is about 0.6% of Ohio's electorate (the `frame_share` of 0.0057 in Table
1.11), and 0.6% of 400 rounds to two twins; this draw got none. No weight can
give an empty cell the right share, so the vote2024 margin cannot close, and
raking it pushes the residual onto ethnicity. This is a hard limit of a small
panel, not something to tune away.

At the project's Tier C size the cell is populated and every margin closes. The
next block rakes `panel_4000` the same way and prints its report:

**Table 1.15.** The raked 4,000-skeleton panel.

```{r rake-4000}
panel_4000[, weight := rake(panel_4000, mini, MARGINS)]
report(panel_4000, mini, "n = 4000")
```

Every line of Table 1.15 reads `0.0000 pp` — the acceptance standard met.

The weights still run wider than the project panel's 0.95–1.04 (the first line
of Table 1.15 gives the range), because a synthetic draw has to correct more: the
registrant draw gets its voter / stay-home split from the file itself, so less
is left for the weight to fix. Trimming the weights, as the project's draw does,
is the last step.

> **This is why Tier C is 4,000.** Not because 4,000 interviews are needed for
> precision on a statewide number — a few hundred would do — but because the
> panel has to be jointly representative on five margins *and* still fill thin
> cells like third-party voters, Asian Ohioans, and 18–24-year-olds who voted.

**A rule you must not break.** The tiers are drawn *self-weighting* — the weight
above only documents the rake. Do **not** re-apply it to tier aggregates, and
cluster any twin-level inference by donor, because donors are reused.

## 7. What the Talking to Machines panel has that yours does not

The project's Ohio statewide panel draws 4,000 **real registrants** into the
same cells. Its **acceptance report** is the summary the project writes every
time it draws a panel: how the draw was set up, how well it matches its targets,
and what it is made of. The block below prints it in full.

**Table 1.16.** The acceptance report of the project's Ohio statewide panel.

```{r real-checks, comment = ""}
cat(readLines(file.path(DATA, "oh_checks_statewide.txt")), sep = "
")
```

The line to read first starts `county margin:` (the fifth line of Table 1.16):
88 counties calibrated to their certified 2024 shares, with a largest county
two-party error of 3.07 points. The block starting `Acceptance — Tier C vs
target margins` is the same audit you ran in Section 6, on the real panel.

Three things to notice.

**Turnout comes from the file, not the frame.** For each group, compare the
turnout your stage-2 frame predicts with the turnout the project's target frame
takes from the Ohio voter file. The block below loads the project's target frame
as `tgt`. It then computes, for each sex, age band and ethnicity, the frame's
turnout (voters over adults in `sf2`, column `frame`) and the file's (the
`voters` column of `tgt` over its `N`, column `file`). Both use the same census
adults as the denominator. (`eth5` merges the two smallest ethnicity groups into
`Other`, to match `tgt`.)

**Table 1.17.** Turnout by group: stage-2 frame against the voter file.

```{r turnout-frame-vs-file}
tgt <- fread(file.path(DATA, "oh_targets_statewide.csv"))
sf2[, eth5 := fifelse(ethnicity %in% c("Native", "Mixed-race"), "Other", ethnicity)]

turnout_by <- function(by) {
  frame <- sf2[, .(frame = sum(N_D + N_R + N_Other) / sum(N)), by = by]
  file  <- tgt[, .(file  = sum(voters) / sum(N)), by = by]
  out   <- merge(frame, file, by = by)
  data.table(variable = by, group = out[[by]],
             frame = round(out$frame, 2), file = round(out$file, 2))
}
rbind(turnout_by("gender"), turnout_by("age_bins"), turnout_by("eth5"))
```

The first two rows of Table 1.17 carry the lesson. The frame puts women's
turnout at 0.58 against 0.67 in the file, and men's at 0.71 against 0.62: it has
the sexes the wrong way round. The CES post-election wave is 95%+ voters, so
*who* abstains is weakly identified. Where a file exists, the file wins.

The project's target is therefore **hybrid**: cell sizes from the ACS, the
voter/stay-home split from the file, the D/R split from the model. Its cells
also carry the county. Note that the two keys are **not nested**: yours has
college and no county, the project's has county and no college, with the vote
class assigned inside each cell. Neither is a coarsening of the other. The next
block prints the first three cells of `tgt`.

**Table 1.18.** `tgt`, the project's target frame: the first three cells.

```{r hybrid-target}
head(tgt, 3)
```

Each row of Table 1.18 is a cell of the project's key: district (`cd`), county,
sex, ethnicity (`eth5`) and age band. `N` is its adults, from the ACS; `voters`
and `stay` split them by 2024 turnout, from the voter file; `D`, `R` and `Other`
split the voters by class, from the model.

**Sex and ethnicity are inferred, and the panel records how.** Ohio's file has
neither. Sex comes from Social Security Administration first-name frequencies;
ethnicity from Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding. The line starting
`provenance:` in Table 1.16 counts both: 3,703 of 4,000 sexes inferred from the
name and 297 assigned within the cell because the name is ambiguous; 3,506
ethnicities taken at the most likely group and 494 drawn in proportion to the
probabilities. Every skeleton records which.

**Partisanship comes from the primary ballot, not registration.** Ohio has no
party registration — its "affiliation" field is the party of the last primary
ballot taken. So the propensity steering which registrant fills a D or an R slot
is estimated from the CES validated *primary* field. The block below prints the
map the panel uses.

**Table 1.19.** The partisan map: one row per type of voter-file record, with
the weight each type gets for a Democratic (`p_D`), Republican (`p_R`) or other
(`p_Other`) slot.

```{r pmap, comment = ""}
cat(readLines(file.path(DATA, "oh_pmap.csv")), sep = "\n")
```

Read the row `D.dp` in Table 1.19 as: a registrant who took a Democratic primary
ballot is given a 0.962 weight for the Democratic slots. A simpler rule would be
two fixed constants, say `.9` and `.05`. Used as competing selection weights,
those are odds of 18:1 and behave as near-certainty rather than as the modest
priors they look like. Estimating the weights per state from the CES validated
file avoids that.

The coherence check is the block headed `partisan_class (primary ballots) by
vote2024` near the end of Table 1.16. In its `D` row, 52% of D-slot twins have
a Democratic primary record (`dem_primary`) against 7% Republican
(`rep_primary`); in its `R` row, 62% of R-slot twins have a Republican record
against 2% Democratic. Note also the `no_primary` column: more than a third of
D-slot twins (37%) have **no** primary record at all — for them the partisan
class rests on the district and county rakes alone.

### Your sample against the real one

Everything above differs, and yet the *composition* should not. Both are drawn
to the same frame, so the vote-class shares of a 4,000-twin synthetic draw and
the project's 4,000-registrant panel should agree with each other, and with the
frame itself, which is the target both were drawn to.

The block below computes the share of each vote class in three places: the
frame (`mini`, column `frame`), your 4,000-skeleton draw (`panel_4000`, column
`yours`), and the project's panel (column `project`). The project's shares are
typed in from Table 1.16: they are the column totals of its block `Tier C:
ethnicity x vote2024 (share of panel)`.

**Table 1.20.** 2024 vote-class shares: frame, your 4,000-skeleton draw, and
the project's panel.

```{r vs-project}
frame_shares <- mini[, .(frame = sum(N) / sum(mini$N)), by = vote2024]
yours <- panel_4000[, .(yours = .N / nrow(panel_4000)), by = vote2024]
frame_shares[, vote2024 := as.character(vote2024)]
yours[, vote2024 := as.character(vote2024)]

# the project's panel, summed off the ethnicity x vote table in the acceptance report
project <- data.table(vote2024 = c("D", "R", "Other", "stay"),
                      project  = c(0.285, 0.356, 0.005, 0.355))

Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "vote2024"), list(frame_shares, yours, project))[
  , .(vote2024, frame = round(frame, 3), yours = round(yours, 3), project)]
```

The three columns of Table 1.20 agree to about a thousandth. The two panels do
not just agree with each other: both agree with the population they were drawn
to. That is what "representation by construction" means: the skeleton source
changes, the population being represented does not.

## 8. Deposit your panel

The last block saves `panel`, your 400 skeletons with their ages and weights,
to `output/oh_mini_panel_400.parquet`, and prints where it wrote the file.

```{r deposit}
dir.create(file.path("..", "output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
out <- file.path("..", "output", "oh_mini_panel_400.parquet")
write_parquet(panel, out)
cat("written:", normalizePath(out, winslash = "/"), "\n")
```

Notebook 2 picks this file up, attaches a CES donor to each skeleton, renders it
as a persona, and interviews it.

## Where this comes from

The frame, the draw and the audit follow the method **Talking to Machines** uses
to build its digital-twin panels for the 2026 races. Talking to Machines is an
international collaboration of academics and industry researchers, directed by
Sonja Vogt (HEC Lausanne) and Ray Duch (Nuffield College, Oxford). Your panel
differs from the project's mainly in the skeleton source (Section 7): synthetic cells
here, real registrants there.
